nodes.label: Fee sniping and incentives
nodes.body: The ninth and tenth sections of the chapter are about adding fees correctly and about the defence against fee sniping with the lock time, which only matters when fees are a large part of the miner's income (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The study computed the subsidy and the fee share of real blocks, measured the lock times of a wallet and of the chain, and found that the book's example of the lock time is off by one block (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This subject covers Block reward mix; Sniping attack; Lock time defense against fee sniping.

nodes.label: Block reward mix
nodes.body: This subject asks what part of a miner's income are fees: the subsidy and its halvings, the fee share of two real blocks and the arguments about a future of fees only (Nakamoto, 2008). It matters because the defence against fee sniping is only needed when fees are large. This subject covers Subsidy halvings; Fees versus subsidy; A future with fees only.

nodes.label: Subsidy halvings
nodes.body: The block subsidy is the amount of new bitcoin that the miner of a block may create in its coinbase transaction; it started at 50 bitcoins and is cut in half every 210,000 blocks, which the book describes in its chapter on mining as 6.25 new bitcoins in 2023 and a coming halving at block 840,000 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the source function GetBlockSubsidy the rule is a shift: the number of halvings is the height divided by 210,000, the starting value is 50 coins, and the value is shifted right by the number of halvings (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The chapter's function gives 5,000,000,000 satoshis at the heights 0 and 209,999, 2,500,000,000 at 210,000, 625,000,000 at 839,999 and 312,500,000 at 840,000 and at the height 971,489 of 2026-10-15. The subsidy matters for this chapter because every halving makes the fees a larger part of what a miner earns (Nakamoto, 2008).
nodes.definition: The subsidy is 50 bitcoins shifted right once per 210,000 blocks (GetBlockSubsidy): 625,000,000 satoshis before block 840,000 and 312,500,000 from it, as in block 971,489.

nodes.label: Fees versus subsidy
nodes.body: The book says in its section on fee sniping that the attack is not very lucrative today because the block subsidy is much higher than the total fees per block, and that at some point in the future fees will be the majority of the reward (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Whether that is true depends on the block. Block 840,000, mined on 2024-04-20, paid its miner 4,075,061,499 satoshis of which 3,762,561,499 (37.6 bitcoins) were fees, only 312,500,000 (3.125 bitcoins) subsidy: the fees were 92.33 percent of the reward. Block 971,489 of 2026-10-15 carried fees of 1,454,221 satoshis against the same subsidy, 0.46 percent (Mempool Space, 2026). The statement of the book is a fair description of an average block and is wrong for the halving block, a correction that the chapter lists among its findings; the share is computed here from the explorer's numbers and the rule of the subsidy (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.label: A future with fees only
nodes.body: Satoshi Nakamoto's paper says that the incentive for miners can also be funded with transaction fees: if the output value of a transaction is less than its input value, the difference is a transaction fee that is added to the incentive value of the block, and once a predetermined number of coins have entered circulation the incentive can transition entirely to fees (Nakamoto, 2008). The book follows this line when it says that the fees become more and more important as the subsidy declines and provide the incentive to continue securing Bitcoin with proof of work (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Carlsten and his coauthors at Princeton asked whether it makes no difference to security whether miners are paid by block rewards or by fees, and showed that it does: with only fees the variance of the reward grows and new strategies appear (Carlsten et al., 2016). The chapter finds both passages in its saved copies of the papers and does not simulate their models; the question is open in the sense that it depends on the future of the fee market. nodes.label: Sniping attack
nodes.body: This subject asks how likely and how dangerous fee sniping is: the formula of its chance and the undercutting attack of the Princeton study (Bitcoin Optech, 2026). It matters because the book calls the attack theoretical, and the numbers show how the chance rises with the hash rate. This subject covers Sniping probability; Undercutting attack.

nodes.label: Sniping probability
nodes.body: Fee sniping is the attack in which a miner deliberately re-mines one or more earlier blocks to take the fees from the miners who first created them, perhaps with a block extending the chain at the same time; the Optech topic page gives the dishonest miner's chance of success, if every other miner is honest, as (x / (1 - x)) squared, where x is the miner's share of the hash rate (Bitcoin Optech, 2026). The formula is small but telling: a miner with a tenth of the hash rate succeeds with probability 1.23 percent, one with 30 percent with 18.37 percent, one with 45 percent with 66.94 percent, and one with half with certainty, since a miner who can out-mine all others combined can always win the race. The chapter computed the values with the formula and does not claim that real miners do this; the book calls it a theoretical attack scenario and the hash rate of single miners is below the levels where the chance is high (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: A miner with a share x of the hash rate wins the race to re-mine the last block and extend it with probability (x / (1 - x)) squared: 1.23 percent for 10 percent, 18.37 percent for 30 percent and 66.94 percent for 45 percent, reaching certainty at one half.

nodes.label: Undercutting attack
nodes.body: In the study On the Instability of Bitcoin Without the Block Reward, Carlsten, Kalodner, Weinberg and Narayanan from Princeton University show that when transaction fees are the only reward, mining honestly may no longer be the best strategy; a miner can profit by forking the head of the chain and leaving the high-fee transactions of the latest block unmined, so that the next blocks collect them, which they call the undercutting attack (Carlsten et al., 2016). The paper's simulator explores strategies and finds that undercutting can be harmful to the stability of Bitcoin consensus, and the authors conclude that the role of block rewards must be rethought. The chapter found the passages in the saved copy of the paper, which is dated 2016 and was presented at the ACM conference on computer and communications security in Vienna; it did not rerun the simulator, and it reports the paper as a reason for the defence in the next leaves (Carlsten et al., 2016). This example reads carlsten_2016_instability.txt, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: True
nodes.example: forking the head to take the transactions
nodes.definition: Carlsten and his coauthors show that with only fees miners profit by forking the head of the chain and leaving out its transactions, which they call undercutting; the passage is found in the saved copy and the attack is not recomputed.

nodes.label: Lock time defense against fee sniping
nodes.body: This subject asks how a wallet defends against fee sniping with the lock time: the rule of Bitcoin Core, its fallback, the use on the real chain, the exact boundary of the consensus rule, the effect of the final sequence and the proposal for taproot (Bitcoin Core, 2026). It matters because the book's example is off by one block, and the correct rule is the one the node enforces. This subject covers Wallet lock time rule; Wallet lag fallback; Share of mainnet transactions with the previous height; Lock time boundary; Final sequence disables lock time; Taproot anti-fee-sniping (BIP 326).

nodes.label: Wallet lock time rule
nodes.body: A lock time is a field of the transaction that says in which block height or at which time the transaction becomes valid. To discourage fee sniping a wallet sets it to the height of the current tip, so that only the next block can include the transaction; the source comment says that a miner who considers fee sniping then has fewer options for pulling off the attack (Bitcoin Core, 2026). In about one case in ten the code subtracts a random number of 0 to 99 blocks, which is good for the privacy of transactions that are broadcast late. The run made 60 payments with the wallet and read their lock times: 56 equal the tip and four were back-dated, by 6, 28, 35 and 54 blocks, all below 100; every one carried the sequence 0xfffffffd. The expected share is 10 percent and the run gave 6.7 percent, which is within the chance of a sample so small. The book recommends this defence for all wallets (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: The wallet sets the lock time to the height of the tip, and in about one case in ten back-dates it by a random 0 to 99 blocks: 56 of 60 transactions in the run had the tip, four were back-dated by 6, 28, 35 and 54.

io.code: s = R['sniping']['samples']; d = sorted(s_['tip'] - s_['locktime'] for s_ in s); (len(s), d.count(0), [x for x in d if x], L.has('core_src_wallet_spend.cpp', 'rng_fast.randrange(100)'))

nodes.label: Wallet lag fallback
nodes.body: The defence only makes sense if the wallet knows the real tip. The source of the wallet defines the function IsCurrentForAntiFeeSniping, which returns false while the node is in initial block download or when the best block is older than 8 hours, a constant MAX_ANTI_FEE_SNIPING_TIP_AGE of 8 x 60 x 60 seconds (Bitcoin Core, 2026). In that case the code sets the lock time to a constant 0, with the comment that this avoids leaking a potentially unique lock time fingerprint, since a wallet with an old tip would write an old height that others do not. The chapter found the constant and the two statements in the saved source and computed 8 x 60 x 60 = 28,800 seconds; the case was not run, because a regtest chain made on the same day is never older than eight hours and the test would only show the same value 0.
nodes.example: a tip older than 8 hours means lock time 0
nodes.definition: When the node is still syncing or its tip is older than 8 hours the wallet sets the lock time to 0, so as not to leak a unique fingerprint.

nodes.label: Share of mainnet transactions with the previous height
nodes.body: Do real wallets use the defence? The chapter counted, in the first 599 transactions after the coinbase of two mainnet blocks, how many carry a lock time equal to the height of the previous block, which is what a wallet that follows the rule writes when the transaction is created while that block is the tip. In block 840,000 (2024-04-20) it was 89 of 599 (15 percent) and in block 971,489 (2026-10-15) 33 of 599 (6 percent); a lock time of 0 was carried by 507 and 563 (Mempool Space, 2026). The share is a lower bound for wallets that follow the rule, because a transaction created some blocks earlier will show an older height, and an upper bound for nothing in particular, because other software may write the same number. The defence is therefore used but not general (Bitcoin Optech, 2026), and BIP 326 mentions that about a fifth of recent transactions had anti-fee-sniping lock times in the author's data (Belcher, 2021).

nodes.definition: On mainnet 89 of the first 599 transactions of block 840,000 (15 percent) and 33 of block 971,489 (6 percent) carry the previous block's height as lock time, and 507 and 563 carry 0.

nodes.label: Lock time boundary
nodes.body: The book sets the lock time of the example to 100,001 when the highest block is 100,000 and says that the transaction can only be included in block 100,001, the next block; the chapter on transactions says that a lock time of 123,456 can be included in block 123,456 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The consensus rule in the function IsFinalTx is different by one: a transaction with a lock time below the height of the block is final, so a lock time equal to the height is not, and the earliest block for a lock time of L is the block L + 1 (Bitcoin Core, 2026); BIP 113 says the same in other words, that a transaction is excluded while the block height is less than or equal to the lock time (Kerin, 2015). The chapter computed the function for 100,001 in block 100,001 (not final) and for 100,000 (final), and ran it: with the tip at 129 a lock time of 130 was refused as non-final by the mempool and a block of height 130 containing it was rejected with bad-txns-nonfinal, while a lock time of 129 was accepted and mined; the wallet, in the run above, used the tip. This is an error of the printed book, and it is not corrected on the development branch.
nodes.definition: A transaction is final in a block when its lock time is below the block's height, so a lock time equal to the height is not: on the node a lock time of the next block's height was refused as non-final and rejected from a block, and the tip's height was accepted.

nodes.label: Final sequence disables lock time
nodes.body: A lock time is only enforced when at least one input of the transaction has a sequence number that is not final; if every input has the sequence 0xffffffff, the transaction is final whatever its lock time says, and the function IsFinalTx returns true after its loop over the inputs (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book's chapter on transactions describes the same: setting the sequence to its maximum value finalizes the transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the run, at the tip 254, a transaction with the lock time 255 and the sequence 0xffffffff was accepted by the mempool, the same transaction with the sequence 0xfffffffd was refused as non-final, the one with lock time equal to the tip was accepted, and after one block (tip 255) the transaction with 255 and 0xfffffffd became acceptable. This is why a wallet that wants the defence against fee sniping must never use the final sequence, and the source asserts it, in the code that sets the lock time (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
nodes.example: tip plus 1 with sequence 0xffffffff is final
nodes.definition: A lock time is ignored when every input has the final sequence 0xffffffff, so a lock time of tip plus 1 was accepted with that sequence and refused with 0xfffffffd, and the same transaction became acceptable one block later.

nodes.label: Taproot anti-fee-sniping (BIP 326)
nodes.body: The lock time field has a disadvantage: it is used by few wallets for other reasons, so it can reveal which software made a transaction. BIP 326 proposes that wallets set the sequence field in their taproot transactions, in place of their regular lock time protection, so that a transaction with a sequence value is not unusual and the anti-fee-sniping protection also works for those who use the sequence of BIP 68 (Belcher, 2021). It argues that with the protection by lock time or sequence the bad miner soon runs out of transactions to put in the first block and has to change the plan. The proposal is for taproot outputs, which the book discusses in other chapters, and it keeps the lock time as well in some transactions, because absolute lock times are still used. The chapter found the passages in the saved copy of the BIP and did not execute the proposal, because Bitcoin Core 31.1 was not shown to implement it.
nodes.definition: BIP 326 proposes that taproot wallets use the sequence field instead of the lock time against fee sniping, so that the lock time does not mark some transactions as unusual; the passage is found in the saved copy and the proposal is not executed.

findings: Background

The chapter holds that a transaction carries no fee field and that the fee is the difference between the inputs and the outputs, paid by the spender and collected by the miner of the block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A parse of the raw bytes of a transaction of the Bitcoin Core 31.1 test chain found version, inputs, outputs and lock time and no fee, and a forgotten change output of a 20-bitcoin input made the node refuse the transaction with max-fee-exceeded (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
Background

The chapter states that the fee is a bid for room in a block, the idea that the original paper already described as an incentive that replaces the subsidy over time (Nakamoto, 2008). A block template of the test node listed ten transactions in descending order of fee rate, from 50 to 1 satoshi per virtual byte (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
Background

The fee market is an economic subject with an early literature: fees depend on size and priority, and a fee market can exist without a block size limit (Moeser and Boehme, 2015); (Rizun, 2015). The chapter is consistent with it, since the chapter ties the fee to the block space a transaction takes up (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Comparative analysis

Erratum: the book's remark that the block subsidy is much higher than the fees is true of some blocks and not of others. In block 840,000, the halving block of 2024-04-20, the fees were 3,762,561,499 satoshis, 92.33 percent of the reward, while in block 971,489 they were 0.46 percent (Mempool Space, 2026); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Comparative analysis

Erratum: the book's summary of the default mempool as about one day's worth of transactions does not match the code, which holds 300 megabytes and forgets a transaction after 336 hours, 14 days; and the glossary's minimum fee of 0.5 millibitcoin, 50,000 satoshis, is a historical value that the node no longer applies (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Comparative analysis

The estimatesmartfee call accepts a target of 1 to 1008 blocks but can look back only as far as its history; on a chain 231 blocks high the target of 144 was answered for 60 blocks, and the default mode has been economical since 28.0, so that the default answer differs from the conservative one at 144 blocks (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2024).
Comparative analysis

The replacement hazards are real and measured: three versions of one payment of 0.4 bitcoin made the payee receive 0.8 bitcoin when a miner kept the first and then mined the last, and a large child pins a parent at a cost of 450,780 satoshis to replace. The replacement cycling attack of 2023 is described in the sources but was not run (Bitcoin Optech, 2023); (Bitcoin Optech, 2026).
Comparative analysis

The incentive question of the last section is modelled by Carlsten and colleagues, who show that a chain without a subsidy is unstable because a miner gains by undercutting the block of a rival (Narayanan, 2016), and the probability that a miner with the hash share x wins a sniping race is (x / (1 - x)) squared: 1.23 percent at 10 percent, 66.94 percent at 45 percent (Carlsten et al., 2016); (Poon and Dryja, 2016).
Conclusion

Erratum: the lock time rule of the book and its chapter 6 is off by one: a transaction is final in a block when its lock time is less than the block height, so a lock time equal to the height of the next block is refused on the node. The wallet sets the lock time to the current height, which 89 of 599 transactions of block 840,000 do (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Kerin, 2015); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Conclusion

Taken together, the chapter's teaching on fees, replacement, child-pays-for-parent and anti-sniping remains right in its principles, but five of its defaults and limits are outdated for Bitcoin Core 28 to 31, and the sources show the direction: policy is moving from fixed limits and opt-in signals to cluster-based rules, TRUC transactions and anchors (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026); (Bitcoin Optech, 2026).
Conclusion

Bitcoin Core's own documentation describes the replacement rules in force, including an incremental relay fee of 0.1 satoshi per virtual byte, so a replacement of a 141-byte transaction that had paid 564 satoshis needed at least 579 satoshis in the run (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Harding, 2015).
Contemporary developments

Erratum: the book defines the fee rate as a transaction's size divided by weight, which is a pure number with no price in it. The fee rate is the fee divided by the size, 2.0 satoshis per virtual byte for the run's 141-byte transaction that paid 282 satoshis, whereas size over weight is 0.2513 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Lombrozo et al., 2015).
Contemporary developments

Changed default: the minimum relay fee rate fell from 1 to 0.1 satoshi per virtual byte in Bitcoin Core 30.0, so that the node accepted 15 satoshis for a 141-byte transaction and refused 14, while the wallet keeps its own minimum of 1 satoshi per virtual byte and refused 0.5 and 0.1 (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025); (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
Contemporary developments

Changed default: full replace-by-fee is the default since Bitcoin Core 28.0, so a transaction that does not signal replaceability is replaced on the 31.1 node, and the option -mempoolfullrbf was removed in 29.0 and is refused by 31.1 with exit code 1. The book describes only the opt-in rule of BIP 125 (Bitcoin Core developers, 2024); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025); (Harding, 2015).
Contemporary developments

The change of the default followed a public discussion in December 2022 in which Peter Todd posted on full replace-by-fee on 2022-12-12 and release 24.0.1 announced the option -mempoolfullrbf (Todd, 2022); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2022); (Bitcoin Optech, 2022).
Contemporary developments

Package relay is partly realized: Bitcoin Core 28.0 accepts a package of one parent and one child through submitpackage, so that a child can pay for a parent that is below the minimum relay fee (the test node took a parent of 0 fee and a child of 10,000 satoshis), while the peer-to-peer ancestor package relay of BIP 331 is still a Draft (Bitcoin Core developers, 2024); (Zhao, 2022).
Contemporary developments

Erratum: the book gives the extra child of the CPFP carve-out as 1,000 virtual bytes and the limit as 100,000, while the code constant EXTRA_DESCENDANT_TX_SIZE_LIMIT is 10,000 and the descendant size limit is 101,000; the carve-out was added in release 0.19.0.1, not 0.19.0, which was tagged and never released (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2019); (Corallo, 2018).
Contemporary developments

Changed policy: the cluster mempool of Bitcoin Core 31.0 replaces the 25-transaction ancestor and descendant limits by a limit of 64 transactions per cluster, and the carve-out of the old limits is removed, and the run shows the quadratic work of the old limits (625 package updates, and 2,500 at double the limit) (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026); (Daftuar et al., 2024).
Contemporary developments

Version-3 (TRUC) transactions of Bitcoin Core 28.0 limit a transaction to one unconfirmed parent and one child, at most 10,000 virtual bytes for the transaction and 1,000 for the child. In the run the cost of replacing a pinned parent fell from 450,780 to 5,145 satoshis, 88 times less than for an unrestricted large child (Zhao, 2024); (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
Contemporary developments

Anchor outputs gained a standard form: the pay-to-anchor output script 51024e73 of BIP 433 can be spent by anyone, and release 29.0 relays a zero-fee parent with an ephemeral dust output when a child spends the dust in the same package. The lightning anchor commitments of BOLT 3 are the application the chapter names (Sanders, 2025); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025); (Lightning developers, 2026).

stories.title: A node that only listens to replacements
stories.who: Peter Todd, a Bitcoin developer who posted the build, and Antoine Riard, whose peering code it contains
stories.where: the bitcoin-dev mailing list, and the nodes of the public Bitcoin network that run Bitcoin Core 24.0.1
stories.story: On Monday 12 December 2022 Peter Todd posted to the bitcoin-dev list a build of Bitcoin Core 24.0.1 with Antoine Riard's full-rbf peering code. Release 24.0.1 had just added the option mempoolfullrbf, which defaults to off and so allows only opt-in replacement. Todd's build advertises a FULL_RBF service bit when the option is set and connects to four additional nodes that do the same, so that a core group of nodes passes on replacements reliably. He estimated about 30 reliable nodes running his branch and about 50 Bitcoin Knots nodes that advertised the bit. Bitcoin Optech's newsletter of 14 December 2022 reported the monitoring of full-rbf replacements, and Bitcoin Core 28.0 later made full replacement the default and 29.0 removed the option. The test node of this chapter accepts a replacement of a transaction that never signalled.
stories.lesson: Policy is what most nodes choose to relay, and it changes by their choice

stories.title: A pre-signed transaction cannot guess next week's fee
stories.who: Matt Corallo, a Bitcoin Core and Lightning developer, writing to the bitcoin-dev and lightning-dev lists
stories.where: the bitcoin-dev and lightning-dev mailing lists, cross-posted; the rule shipped in Bitcoin Core 0.19.0.1
stories.story: On Thursday 29 November 2018 Matt Corallo wrote that Lightning channels exchange pre-signed transactions that are broadcast much later, so their fee has to be predicted or added afterwards by a child. He described how a counterparty could chain a large child of only moderate fee rate to the anyone-can-spend output of a commitment transaction and keep it at the bottom of the mempool. His answer, the carve-out, allowed one extra small child beyond the usual limits, and he proposed that it be no greater than 1K in virtual size. Bitcoin Core 0.19.0.1 shipped the carve-out in November 2019 with an extra child of up to 10,000 virtual bytes, and Bitcoin Core 31.0 removed it with the cluster mempool. The book states 1,000 and 100,000 where the code says 10,000 and 101,000.
stories.lesson: A limit built for one attack can outlive the problem it solved

stories.title: The block in which fees were nearly the whole reward
stories.who: the mining pool ViaBTC, which found block 840,000, and the Bitcoin Core rule that halves the subsidy every 210,000 blocks
stories.where: the Bitcoin chain at height 840,000, the block of the fourth halving
stories.story: Block 840,000 was found on 20 April 2024 at 00:09 UTC by the pool ViaBTC and held 3,050 transactions. It was the first block after the fourth halving, so the subsidy fell from 6.25 to 3.125 bitcoins, 312,500,000 satoshis. The fees in the same block were 3,762,561,499 satoshis, so the reward of 4,075,061,499 satoshis was 92.33 percent fees. In block 971,489 the fees were only 0.46 percent of the reward. The book says that the subsidy is much higher than the fees, which is true of that later block and false of the halving block.
stories.lesson: Check a book's claim against the block, because the market moves

stories.title: What if nobody got a subsidy?
stories.who: Miles Carlsten, Harry Kalodner, S. Matthew Weinberg and Arvind Narayanan, computer scientists at Princeton University
stories.where: Princeton University, New Jersey; the paper was presented at ACM CCS, the week after the announcement
stories.story: On 21 October 2016 Arvind Narayanan announced on the Princeton CITP blog the paper On the Instability of Bitcoin Without the Block Reward, written with Miles Carlsten, Harry Kalodner and Matt Weinberg and presented at ACM CCS the next week. They start from the observation that Bitcoin gives miners two incentives, block rewards and transaction fees, and that the first is expected to give way to the second. Their model shows that when fees are the main income a miner can gain by undercutting a block of a rival, which makes mining less stable. The chapter's last section describes the same pressure as fee sniping, and the run computes that a miner with 45 percent of the hash rate wins the race to re-mine a block with probability 66.94 percent. The wallet's countermeasure is the lock time of the current height.
stories.lesson: Fees must replace the subsidy, so the rules for fees must be stable

lecture.title: Chapter 9: Transaction Fees
lecture.say: This deck explains transaction fees: who pays them, how they are priced, how a payment is replaced or bumped, and what changed since the book went to print. Every number on a result picture was computed with the chapter's own Python library. Bitcoin Core 31.1 was run once on a test network, and its answers are only read back, so they are labelled as recorded. The course page for chapter 9 carries the full text, the sources and the code that runs.
lecture.takeaway: Who pays a fee, how it is priced, replaced and bumped, and what moved since print

lecture.title: Today's route through seven parts
lecture.say: The route has seven parts that follow the order of the chapter. Four true stories and twenty-seven code examples are spread across them. The examples are listed in the same order in the chapter code tab of the course page, so every listing in this deck can be run and edited there. Each part opens with a divider that states, in one line, what the part establishes, and closes with the example that proves it.
lecture.takeaway: Seven parts, twenty-seven examples, four true stories

lecture.title: The questions this chapter answers
lecture.say: The seven questions are the chapter's own, rewritten so that each has an answer on a slide of this deck. They cover who pays a fee, how a fee rate is computed, how a node estimates a rate, what a replacement must pay, how a child pays for its parent, how a family can pin a payment, and what fee sniping is. A reader who can answer all seven has understood the chapter, and the summary returns to them.
lecture.takeaway: Each has an answer on a slide; we return to them in the summary

lecture.title: One chapter, seven parts
lecture.say: The chapter has seven parts and thirty-one key concepts. Each part gets a divider, concept cards with literal meanings, code that runs, and some parts a true story. The deck follows the order of the chapter, so the map on this slide is also the table of contents of the course page. The numbers under each part count the concepts and the examples that belong to it.
lecture.takeaway: Seven parts; every slide today lives on this map

lecture.title: Who pays the fee
lecture.say: A transaction has no fee field. The fee is what the inputs hold and the outputs do not claim, so the spender pays it and only the spender can change it. This part shows how to see that in the raw bytes, what goes wrong when the change output is forgotten, and why nobody else can add to the fee of a signed payment. The three examples of the part are computed from one recorded run of Bitcoin Core.
lecture.takeaway: The spender pays the fee, like a tip left on the counter.

lecture.title: Who pays the fee: key concepts (1 of 3)
lecture.say: These cards cover Adding Fees to Transactions, Who Pays the Transaction Fee?, absurd fees and change output. Each card names one concept of the chapter and gives its meaning in one sentence. Read the meaning, retell it in your own words, and connect it with the concepts on the neighbouring cards. These concepts are the vocabulary that the code slides of the same part use, so a card that is clear here makes the listing easier to read. The full explanation, with the code that runs, is on the course page for chapter 9.
lecture.takeaway: Read the idea, then run the example that proves it

lecture.title: A fee is a difference, not a field
lecture.say: A transaction lists its inputs and its outputs, and nothing else. The miner's fee is whatever the inputs hold and the outputs do not claim. The listing parses the raw bytes of one real payment with the chapter's own parser and finds no fee field. The inputs hold 2,000,000,000 satoshis and the outputs claim 100,000,000, so 1,900,000,000 satoshis are left over for the miner. It is example 1 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Nothing in the transaction states the fee: it is inputs minus outputs

lecture.title: Who pays the fee: key concepts (2 of 3)
lecture.say: These cards cover excessive fees, fees, inputs and outputs. Each card names one concept of the chapter and gives its meaning in one sentence. Read the meaning, retell it in your own words, and connect it with the concepts on the neighbouring cards. These concepts are the vocabulary that the code slides of the same part use, so a card that is clear here makes the listing easier to read. The full explanation, with the code that runs, is on the course page for chapter 9.
lecture.takeaway: Read the idea, then run the example that proves it

lecture.title: What a forgotten change output costs
lecture.say: If a wallet forgets the change output, the difference between inputs and outputs becomes an enormous fee. The node refuses the payment with the reason max-fee-exceeded, which is a safety limit and not a consensus rule. Mined with that limit lifted, the miner's reward equals the subsidy plus the fee, which shows where the money went. It is example 2 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: A safety limit protects the spender from paying nearly everything as fee

lecture.title: Who pays the fee: key concepts (3 of 3)
lecture.say: These cards cover overpaying transaction fees, payments, transaction fees and transactions. Each card names one concept of the chapter and gives its meaning in one sentence. Read the meaning, retell it in your own words, and connect it with the concepts on the neighbouring cards. These concepts are the vocabulary that the code slides of the same part use, so a card that is clear here makes the listing easier to read. The full explanation, with the code that runs, is on the course page for chapter 9.
lecture.takeaway: Read the idea, then run the example that proves it

lecture.title: Only the spender can raise the fee
lecture.say: The listing cuts the first output of a signed payment by 5,000 satoshis. The node rejects the copy because the signature covers the amounts and no longer fits. So the fee belongs to the spender: anyone else who wants a payment confirmed sooner must pay in a second transaction, which is the idea of child pays for parent in a later part. It is example 3 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: The signature covers the amounts, so nobody else can add to the fee

lecture.title: Fees and fee rates
lecture.say: Miners are paid by the space a payment takes, not by its value. This part measures size, weight and virtual size, turns a fee into a rate, and meets the floors that nodes, wallets and dust rules set. Block space is limited, so the fee rate is the unit in which payments compete. The five examples of the part measure one payment, one block and three kinds of minimum.
lecture.takeaway: A fee is a bill, and the rate is its price per unit of space.

lecture.title: Fees and fee rates: key concepts
lecture.say: These cards cover Fees and Fee Rates, blocks and fee rates. Each card names one concept of the chapter and gives its meaning in one sentence. Read the meaning, retell it in your own words, and connect it with the concepts on the neighbouring cards. These concepts are the vocabulary that the code slides of the same part use, so a card that is clear here makes the listing easier to read. The full explanation, with the code that runs, is on the course page for chapter 9.
lecture.takeaway: Read the idea, then run the example that proves it

lecture.title: Size, weight and virtual size
lecture.say: One payment has 113 bytes without witness data and 222 bytes in all. Its weight is 561 units, because witness bytes count one each and the other bytes four. Its virtual size is 141, the weight over four rounded up. Fees and block space are measured in this unit, so two payments with the same value can differ in cost. It is example 4 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Fees are charged per virtual byte, which is the weight over four

lecture.title: A fee rate and its units
lecture.say: The rate is the fee over the virtual size: 282 satoshis over 141 virtual bytes gives 2 satoshis per byte. Some tools speak in coins per thousand bytes, so 0.0000657 means 6.57 satoshis per byte. Two spellings of ten satoshis per byte give the same fee, and a wrong factor gives an absurd one, which is why the units must always be written next to the number. It is example 5 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Mixing the units changes the fee by a factor of a hundred thousand

lecture.title: Space in a block is limited
lecture.say: The consensus limit is four million units of weight per block. Block 840,000 weighs 3,993,281 units, which is 99.83 percent of the limit. When blocks are full, payments must bid for room, and the fee rate is the bid. The limit is a constant in the saved source of Bitcoin Core, so the listing reads it from there instead of typing it. It is example 6 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: A full block makes fee rates compete

lecture.title: The minimum relay fee
lecture.say: A node relays only payments above its floor, here a tenth of a satoshi per byte. For 141 bytes that is 14.1 satoshis, so payments of 8 and 14 satoshis are refused and one of 15 is accepted. The floor protects nodes from spam, and it is policy, not consensus: another node may set it differently. It is example 7 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: A fee below the floor is not relayed, however valid the payment

lecture.title: Dust and the wallet's floor
lecture.say: An output is dust when spending it would cost more than it holds. The limit is three satoshis for each byte of the output plus its spending input, which gives 294 satoshis for the common segwit key output. The anchor output is the smallest limit of the three. The wallet in this run also refuses rates below one satoshi per byte. It is example 8 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Wallets keep stricter floors than nodes; dust is a floor on outputs

lecture.title: Fee estimation from past blocks
lecture.say: A wallet must guess a rate that will confirm in time. This part shows how the estimator learns from past blocks, where its answers stop, and how two real blocks show a market that moves by a factor of five hundred. An estimate is a summary of what earlier blocks confirmed, so it can only be as good as the history it has seen. The three examples of the part use one recorded run and the census of two mainnet blocks.
lecture.takeaway: Estimating a fee is guessing the fare from past journeys.

lecture.title: Fee estimation: key concepts
lecture.say: These cards cover Bitcoin Core and Estimating Appropriate Fee Rates. Each card names one concept of the chapter and gives its meaning in one sentence. Read the meaning, retell it in your own words, and connect it with the concepts on the neighbouring cards. These concepts are the vocabulary that the code slides of the same part use, so a card that is clear here makes the listing easier to read. The full explanation, with the code that runs, is on the course page for chapter 9.
lecture.takeaway: Read the idea, then run the example that proves it

lecture.title: An estimate needs history
lecture.say: A node without history answers an estimate request with an error: insufficient data. After 120 rounds of test traffic it can estimate, here about 1.2 satoshis per byte at every target tried. The estimate is a summary of what past blocks confirmed, so a new node cannot yet say what a fee should be. It is example 9 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: The estimator answers only from blocks it has seen

lecture.title: How far the estimator can see
lecture.say: Asked for a target of 144 blocks, the node answers with the 60 blocks it can see. The default mode equals the economical mode at every target tried. The conservative mode is more cautious and answers differently at the longest target, so a wallet should choose the mode that fits its risk. It is example 10 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: The estimator cannot see further than its data; the modes differ in caution

lecture.title: Two blocks, two fee markets
lecture.say: The census holds the 599 highest-paying payments of the halving block 840,000 and of block 971,489. The median rate in the first was 1,436.45 satoshis per byte and in the second 3.02. A fee estimate is only as good as the market it was learned in, because the same payment would have cost a factor of five hundred less in the second block. It is example 11 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: The market moved from over a thousand satoshis per byte to three

lecture.title: Replace by fee (RBF)
lecture.say: A payment that waits too long can be replaced by a copy that pays more. This part runs the signal that invites replacement, the rules a replacement must meet, the default that changed in release 28.0, and the hazards of replacing. The rules are policy, so they changed with releases of Bitcoin Core. The four examples of the part replace payments on a test network.
lecture.takeaway: Replacing a payment is raising your bid at an auction.

lecture.title: Replace by fee (RBF): key concepts
lecture.say: These cards cover BIP 125 opt-in replaceability signal, Replace By Fee (RBF) Fee Bumping, conflicting transactions and fee bumping. Each card names one concept of the chapter and gives its meaning in one sentence. Read the meaning, retell it in your own words, and connect it with the concepts on the neighbouring cards. These concepts are the vocabulary that the code slides of the same part use, so a card that is clear here makes the listing easier to read. The full explanation, with the code that runs, is on the course page for chapter 9.

lecture.title: The opt-in replacement signal
lecture.say: A payment signals that it may be replaced when one of its inputs has a sequence number below 0xfffffffe. In the halving block 485 of 599 payments signalled; in block 971,489 only 273. The signal matters less now that replacement needs no signal, but it still tells other software what the sender intends. It is example 12 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Any input with a sequence below 0xfffffffe signals replaceability

lecture.title: A replacement must pay enough
lecture.say: A replacement must pay more than the payment it replaces, and it must also pay for its own size at the incremental rate. For a payment of 564 satoshis and 141 bytes the least acceptable fee is 579. The copies at 514, 564 and 578 are refused, and the one at 579 is accepted. The listing sends four conflicting copies of one payment to the node and records whether each is accepted. It is example 13 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Pay the old fee plus the new size at the incremental rate

lecture.title: Full replacement is the default
lecture.say: The first payment used the final sequence number, so it never asked to be replaceable. A conflicting payment replaced it anyway. Release 28.0 made full replacement the default and release 29.0 removed the option, so starting the node with it off now fails. The book describes the older rule, so this is a change since print. It is example 14 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Bitcoin Core 31.1 replaces without a signal and has no switch to stop it

lecture.title: A node that only listens to replacements
lecture.say: This is a true story, dated 12 December 2022. Peter Todd posted to the bitcoin-dev list a build of Bitcoin Core 24.0.1 that carries Antoine Riard's full-rbf peering code, so that nodes willing to replace could find each other. The lesson is that policy is what most nodes choose to relay, and it changes by their choice. The picture is a stand-in; the link leads to the post.
lecture.takeaway: Peter Todd's build, 12 December 2022

lecture.title: Paying the payee twice
lecture.say: Three versions of a payment replace each other in turn. Versions 0 and 2 do not conflict, so once version 0 is mined, version 2 can be mined as well. The payee asked for 40,000,000 satoshis and received 80,000,000, so the sender pays twice. This is a hazard of replacement for the sender for the payee. It is example 15 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Replacing is not undoing: an old version may still be mined

lecture.title: Is a rule policy or consensus?
lecture.say: Most rules of this chapter are policy: the relay floor, the replacement rules, the version 3 limits and the cluster limits. A payment that breaks them can still be valid in a block that a miner builds. Policy changes with a release of the software, which each node operator may or may not install; consensus changes only by a fork, which every node must follow. The block weight limit is the one consensus rule of the part.
lecture.takeaway: Policy can change with a release; consensus changes only by a fork

lecture.title: Child pays for parent (CPFP)
lecture.say: When the parent cannot be changed, a child can pay for it. This part measures the package rate, shows why nodes now relay packages, and meets the cluster mempool that replaced the old chain limits. A child spends an output of the parent and pays a fee large enough for both, so miners take the pair together. The five examples of the part run on a test network of Bitcoin Core.
lecture.takeaway: A child pays for its parent, like a friend who covers your fare.

lecture.title: Child pays for parent (CPFP): key concepts
lecture.say: These cards cover Child Pays for Parent (CPFP) Fee Bumping, Package Relay, ancestor fee rate mining and package fee rate. Each card names one concept of the chapter and gives its meaning in one sentence. Read the meaning, retell it in your own words, and connect it with the concepts on the neighbouring cards. These concepts are the vocabulary that the code slides of the same part use, so a card that is clear here makes the listing easier to read. The full explanation, with the code that runs, is on the course page for chapter 9.
lecture.takeaway: Read the idea, then run the example that proves it

lecture.title: A child lifts its parent
lecture.say: A parent pays 1 satoshi per byte and would wait a long time. Its child pays 100. Miners treat the pair as one package of 50.77 satoshis per byte, which beats a waiting payment at 20, so the pair is mined first. The listing reads the fees and sizes that the node reports for each entry and divides them. It is example 16 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Miners price a parent and its child as one package

lecture.title: A weak child does not help
lecture.say: This time the child pays only 5 satoshis per byte. The pair together pays 3.02, less than the waiting payment A at 20. Miners took A and left the pair out of the block. A child must pay enough to lift the whole package above the competition, so the fee of the child is chosen from the size of both transactions. It is example 17 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: A package is only as good as its combined rate

lecture.title: Package relay judges a pair together
lecture.say: A parent with a fee of 8 satoshis fails the relay floor of 15 on its own, and its child cannot be sent first because the parent is unknown. As a package the pair is judged by its combined rate and accepted. Limited package relay of one parent and one child exists since release 28.0. The listing records the answer for the parent alone, for the child alone and for the package. It is example 18 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Nodes can judge a pair that a single payment would fail

lecture.title: Cluster limits of the mempool
lecture.say: Release 31.0 groups connected payments into clusters, limited to 64 payments and 101,000 virtual bytes. Of a chain of 65, 64 are accepted and the next is refused as a too-large cluster. The old limit of 25 ancestors is gone, so a chain of 26 is accepted. The limits are policy and can change again. It is example 19 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Limits are set on clusters of connected payments, not on single chains

lecture.title: Mempool size and expiry
lecture.say: The mempool holds 300 megabytes by default. A payment that waits too long is dropped after 336 hours, which is 14 days. The book speaks of about a day's worth, which describes neither default. The listing reads both defaults from the saved source of Bitcoin Core and converts the expiry into days. It is example 20 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: A payment may wait fourteen days, not one

lecture.title: Pinning, anchors and fee bumping
lecture.say: A large child can make a parent costly to replace, and a pre-signed payment cannot guess a future fee. This part runs the carve-out, the version 3 limits and the pay-to-anchor output that answer both problems. Each of them is policy that was added to keep a fee bump possible when the fee is not known in advance. The four examples of the part are followed by the story of the carve-out.
lecture.takeaway: Pinning is a lorry parked behind your car; an anchor is a spare handle.

lecture.title: Pinning and anchors: key concepts
lecture.say: These cards cover CPFP Carve Out and Anchor Outputs and Transaction Pinning. Each card names one concept of the chapter and gives its meaning in one sentence. Read the meaning, retell it in your own words, and connect it with the concepts on the neighbouring cards. These concepts are the vocabulary that the code slides of the same part use, so a card that is clear here makes the listing easier to read. The full explanation, with the code that runs, is on the course page for chapter 9.
lecture.takeaway: Read the idea, then run the example that proves it

lecture.title: A big child pins its parent
lecture.say: A parent that pays 705 satoshis gets a child of 90,012 bytes. To replace the parent, the replacer must pay for the whole family: 450,780 satoshis. With a version 3 child, capped at 1,000 bytes, the same replacement costs 5,145 satoshis, about 88 times less. That is why the cap bounds pinning. It is example 21 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Cap the size of the child and pinning becomes cheap to undo

lecture.title: TRUC limits on a family
lecture.say: A version 3 parent may have one child of at most 1,000 virtual bytes. A child of 1,350 is refused and one of 141 is accepted. A second child at the same rate is refused, and one at a higher rate evicts its sibling, so a pin cannot last. The rules are called topologically restricted until confirmation, which is the long name of version 3 payments. It is example 22 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Strict limits make the worst case of pinning small and known

lecture.title: Pay to anchor: a spendable output
lecture.say: The parent has a zero-value output with the script 51024e73, which anyone can spend, and it pays no fee. Alone the node refuses it. The child spends the anchor with an empty witness and pays 10,000 satoshis, so the package is accepted. This is the form that Lightning channels use to add the fee after the payment was signed. It is example 23 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: The parent pays nothing; the child brings the fee when it is needed

lecture.title: The carve-out limit in the code
lecture.say: The carve-out allowed one extra child beyond the usual limits. The book gives its size as 1,000 virtual bytes, while the source code says 10,000. Release 31.0 removed the rule, because the cluster limits replaced the descendant limits that it worked around. The listing reads the limit from the saved source file and compares it with the book. It is example 24 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Check the numbers of a book against the source code

lecture.title: A pre-signed payment cannot guess its fee
lecture.say: This is a true story, dated 29 November 2018. Matt Corallo wrote that Lightning channels exchange pre-signed transactions that are broadcast much later, so their fee has to be predicted or added afterwards by a child. The lesson is that a limit built for one attack can outlive the problem it solved. The picture is a stand-in; the link leads to the proposal on the mailing list.
lecture.takeaway: Matt Corallo's proposal, 29 November 2018

lecture.title: Fee sniping and incentives
lecture.say: A block pays a subsidy and fees, and the mix changes. When fees dominate, a miner may gain by re-mining a block. This part computes the odds of winning such a race and shows how wallets defend with the lock time. The three examples of the part use the census of two real blocks and the recorded run of Bitcoin Core on a test network.
lecture.takeaway: Fee sniping is a thief rewriting the last page of the ledger.

Read the meaning, retell it in your own words, and connect it with the concepts on the neighbouring cards. These concepts are the vocabulary that the code slides of the same part use, so a card that is clear here makes the listing easier to read. The full explanation, with the code that runs, is on the course page for chapter 9.

lecture.title: Fees against the subsidy
lecture.say: In block 840,000 the fees were 3,762,561,499 satoshis of a 4,075,061,499 reward, so the subsidy of 312,500,000 was only the rest. That is 92.33 percent fees. In block 971,489 fees were 0.46 percent of the reward. The two blocks come from the census saved with the page, so every figure can be recomputed. It is example 25 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: The claim that the subsidy dwarfs fees fails in the halving block

lecture.title: Block 840,000: fees were nearly the reward
lecture.say: This is a true story, dated 20 April 2024. Block 840,000 was found at 00:09 UTC by the pool ViaBTC and held 3,050 transactions. It was the first block after the fourth halving, and its fees were nearly the whole reward. The lesson is to check a book's claim against the block, because the market moves. The picture is a stand-in; the link leads to the block.
lecture.takeaway: ViaBTC and block 840,000, 20 April 2024

lecture.title: Odds of winning a sniping race
lecture.say: A miner with a share x of the hash rate wins the race to re-mine a block with probability x over one minus x, squared. That is 1.23 percent at 10 percent of the hash rate and 66.94 percent at 45 percent. At half the hash rate the chance is certain. The listing computes the formula with the chapter library for four shares. It is example 26 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: With 45 percent of the hash rate a miner wins two races in three

lecture.title: What if nobody got a subsidy?
lecture.say: This is a true story, dated 21 October 2016. Arvind Narayanan announced on the Princeton CITP blog the paper On the Instability of Bitcoin Without the Block Reward, written with Miles Carlsten, Harry Kalodner and Matt Weinberg and presented at ACM CCS the next week. When fees are the main income, a miner can gain by undercutting a rival's block. The link leads to the blog post.
lecture.takeaway: A Princeton paper, 21 October 2016

lecture.title: Wallets lock to the chain tip
lecture.say: A wallet sets the lock time of a payment to the current height, so that a miner who rewrites the block cannot take it. Of 60 payments in the test, 56 sit at the tip and four are set back. Such a payment is not final in the block of that height. The result table also counts the payments of the two census blocks whose lock time is the tip. It is example 27 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: A lock time equal to the tip makes a re-mined block useless to the sniper

# An independent parser reads the raw bytes of one transaction.

late = L.is_final(100001, 100001, [0xfffffffd])
